title: Day 5 of making a cozy RTS where fluffy animals fight bugs, built with Claude, ChatGPT and Meshy
author: FluffyBugGames
selftext:
I grew up on red alert and AoE and always wanted a cozy version, so I’m making one: fluffy animals vs bugs. Hamster knights, frogs and badgers on one side, bees, spiders and grubs on the other. There are 6 clans so far, with fish in fishbowls coming next.

Here’s how the AI side actually works for me. Claude Code writes basically all the code. It’s a browser game in three.js, and Claude also built the multiplayer lobby, the android app and the auto updates. I don’t write code myself, I just describe what I want and test it on my phone. The surprising part is how well it handles big stuff like a whole faction. It’s the tiny visual stuff that takes forever, like a button being a few pixels off.

For art, ChatGPT makes the concepts, then Meshy turns them into 3D. That’s where most of my time goes, because the models never come out game ready. Spiders came out with 7 legs, wings were fused to bodies, and bags floated off characters. I ended up having Claude build me a little model viewer where I can sculpt, paint and pose things to fix them by hand.

The biggest lesson so far: AI art drifts like crazy between generations. What fixed it was always going concept → T-pose sheet → props sheet → 3D, with a written style guide I paste every time. Without that, every faction looked like a different game.

It’s playable in browser and on android. I’ll drop the link in the comments.

Curious how others handle consistency across a lot of AI generated characters. Do you use a style guide, reference sheets, or something else?
